main.title: Custom Robo Arena
main.subtitle: A school day can end in a robot duel
main.summary: Custom Robo Arena is Noise's Nintendo DS action role-playing game about a young Robo Commander building a reputation in the town of Midheart. Meeting other battlers, entering competitions and confronting the misuse of Robo technology connect the small mechanical contests with a larger adventure. The robot's equipment can be changed before entering a real-time arena fight. Moving between town life and those duels gives the collection of parts a practical destination: another opponent will test the machine the player has assembled and the skill with which it is controlled.

cards.heading: A school day can end in a robot duel
cards.text: Custom Robo Arena is Noise's Nintendo DS action role-playing game about a young Robo Commander building a reputation in the town of Midheart. Meeting other battlers, entering competitions and confronting the misuse of Robo technology connect the small mechanical contests with a larger adventure. The robot's equipment can be changed before entering a real-time arena fight. Moving between town life and those duels gives the collection of parts a practical destination: another opponent will test the machine the player has assembled and the skill with which it is controlled.

cards.heading: Five parts define the machine
cards.text: A Robo is built from a body, gun, bomb, pod and legs. Changing those components alters its movement, its available attacks and the range at which it is comfortable fighting. A fast machine with short-range weapons presents a different problem from one prepared to maintain distance. The arena then asks the player to use that arrangement while avoiding the opponent's attacks. Customisation therefore involves deciding how the parts work together, rather than treating every newly acquired component as an automatic improvement over whatever was fitted before it.

cards.heading: The garage continues the battle
cards.text: Between encounters, the garage allows parts to be changed and arrangements to be prepared for another opponent. The wider adventure supplies new rivals and reasons to revisit that equipment, while multiplayer allows another human player to test it in a direct contest. The touchscreen also provides access to the Soulboost ability during a fight. Custom Robo Arena makes the small robot both a fighting character and a personal construction: its performance depends on the decisions made before the duel as well as the movement and timing used after the arena opens.

main.title: Ace Combat X: Skies of Deception
main.subtitle: A squadron takes the war onto a handheld
main.summary: Ace Combat X: Skies of Deception is Namco Bandai and Access Games' PSP aerial combat game, first released in North America on 23 October 2006. The player leads Gryphus Squadron of the Aurelian Air Force through a campaign of air and ground attacks. It is the series' first PSP entry, carrying its mixture of accessible flight, mission briefings and military fiction into a portable format. A small aircraft remains part of a larger conflict, with the player choosing how to approach an operation before bringing the selected weapons and manoeuvres to bear on its targets.

cards.heading: A squadron takes the war onto a handheld
cards.text: Ace Combat X: Skies of Deception is Namco Bandai and Access Games' PSP aerial combat game, first released in North America on 23 October 2006. The player leads Gryphus Squadron of the Aurelian Air Force through a campaign of air and ground attacks. It is the series' first PSP entry, carrying its mixture of accessible flight, mission briefings and military fiction into a portable format. A small aircraft remains part of a larger conflict, with the player choosing how to approach an operation before bringing the selected weapons and manoeuvres to bear on its targets.

cards.heading: Return to the mission with another aircraft
cards.text: Campaign progress unlocks operations for Free Mission, allowing the player to revisit a known objective for a better rank or more points. Those rewards can purchase aircraft and equipment, connecting a successful sortie to the options available later. The player learns which threats deserve attention first and how an approach can leave more room for the next turn. Air targets and ground installations ask for different positioning, so the same aircraft must be understood in relation to the work ahead. Familiarity makes the operation more deliberate rather than simply easier to survive.

cards.heading: A familiar campaign built for PSP
cards.text: Masanori Kato directed and designed the game, with Tamio Kanaji writing its story. The music is credited to Akira Yamasaki, Hitoshi Akiyama, Seiji Koike and Maiko Iuchi, with Yuji Takenouchi supervising after other commitments prevented him from composing. Japanese and European releases followed shortly after North America in 2006. Multiplayer adds another use for the aircraft beyond the campaign. The handheld entry preserves the series' central relationship between pilot, equipment and objective, giving players a complete aerial-combat journey that can be carried away from the television.

main.title: Golden Joystick Awards 2006
main.summary: The Golden Joystick Awards, with every category winner of the 2006 edition.

cards.heading: The players' awards
cards.text: The Golden Joystick Awards celebrate games through a public vote, bringing players into the choice of each year's winners. The awards began in Britain with the 1983 season and later reached an international audience through online voting. Their changing categories trace the growth of games: home computers and consoles, handhelds, online play, independent studios, performance and music. Alongside the public vote, special honours recognise individual contributions to the industry. Each edition preserves its own category names, so the results also show what players and the awards organisers considered worth celebrating at the time.

main.title: Need for Speed: Carbon
main.summary: Need for Speed: Carbon is a 2006 racing video game and the tenth installment in the Need for Speed series.

cards.heading: A new street-racing contest after Most Wanted
cards.text: Need for Speed: Carbon is EA Black Box's 2006 street-racing game, published by Electronic Arts. It followed Most Wanted on home consoles and computers, arriving across the PlayStation 2, Xbox, GameCube, Xbox 360, PlayStation 3 and Wii generations. A separate portable game, Carbon: Own the City, used a different setting and story, with changes to its teammates and mechanics.

cards.heading: Crews compete for Palmont City
cards.text: Carbon's storyline takes place after the events of Need for Speed: Most Wanted, and sees players conducting illegal street races within the fictional city of Palmont City. The story focuses on the player's character taking control of the city from various street-racing gangs. While the gameplay is similar to its predecessor, Carbon introduced a number of new features, including crews and racing wingmen, Touge-styled racing events, and greater customization options.

cards.heading: Reception and the Collector's Edition
cards.text: Upon the release of Carbon, the game received positive reviews from critics, though it faced some criticism over elements of its gameplay mechanics, including a lack of emphasis on police chases compared to its predecessor. A special Collector's Edition version was also released for PlayStation 2, Windows and Xbox 360. It included additional content; such as new cars, new customization items and new events for two of its game modes. As of 2021, download versions of the game are no longer available for purchase in any online stores, and online play was shut down on September 1.

main.title: Killzone: Liberation
main.subtitle: Killzone steps back from the soldier's eyes
main.summary: Killzone: Liberation is Guerrilla Games' PSP action game, first released in North America on 31 October 2006. Templar returns after the original Killzone, undertaking missions against the Helghast that involve rescuing hostages and gathering intelligence. An elevated viewpoint replaces the earlier first-person perspective, giving the player a clearer view of the surrounding ground and enemy positions. The change suits a handheld with a different control arrangement while keeping the war and its visual identity recognisable. The player reads an encounter from above before deciding how Templar should move through it.

cards.heading: Killzone steps back from the soldier's eyes
cards.text: Killzone: Liberation is Guerrilla Games' PSP action game, first released in North America on 31 October 2006. Templar returns after the original Killzone, undertaking missions against the Helghast that involve rescuing hostages and gathering intelligence. An elevated viewpoint replaces the earlier first-person perspective, giving the player a clearer view of the surrounding ground and enemy positions. The change suits a handheld with a different control arrangement while keeping the war and its visual identity recognisable. The player reads an encounter from above before deciding how Templar should move through it.

cards.heading: Use the view to choose a better approach
cards.text: Enemy positions and the shape of the environment become visible together, making movement between useful positions part of the shooting. The player can judge a route before committing to it, then respond when an opponent changes the situation. Mission objectives provide more direction than simply clearing every hostile figure from the screen. A rescue or intelligence task gives a particular place a purpose, encouraging the player to understand how to reach it. The higher camera makes that planning readable, turning a console shooting series into a more compact tactical action format.

cards.heading: A portable continuation with its own identity
cards.text: Mathijs de Jonge directed the project at Guerrilla. The campaign and multiplayer gave PSP players another way to enter Killzone's setting between the larger console releases. Reviews generally praised the handling and presentation, recognising that the change of viewpoint served the new format rather than reducing it to a smaller copy. A later emulated edition reached PlayStation 4 and PlayStation 5 in 2023. Liberation remains the series' only PSP instalment, showing how a familiar world can support a different kind of play when the camera and controls are designed together for the machine.

main.title: Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories
main.summary: Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories is a 2006 action-adventure game developed by Rockstar Leeds and Rockstar North, and published by Rockstar Games.

cards.heading: Vic Vance in the Vice City of 1984
cards.text: Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories is a 2006 action-adventure game developed by Rockstar Leeds and Rockstar North, and published by Rockstar Games. The tenth entry in the Grand Theft Auto series, the game was initially released as a PlayStation Portable exclusive in October 2006. A PlayStation 2 port was released in March 2007. Set within the fictional Vice City (based on Miami) in 1984, the game is a prequel to 2002's Grand Theft Auto: Vice City (set in 1986) and follows the exploits of ex-soldier Victor "Vic" Vance, a minor character originally featured in said game. The story centres around Vic's attempts to build up a criminal empire alongside his brother Lance. With the initial intention of raising money for his sick brother Pete's medication, Vic comes into conflict with rival gangs, drug lords and other enemies.

cards.heading: Taking businesses and playing together
cards.text: In addition to the traditional gameplay elements and side missions of the series, the game features a unique empire building system, in which players must expand their criminal syndicate from the ground-up by taking over businesses from rival organizations, and completing missions specific for each of them to increase their income and unlock additional rewards. Like its predecessor, Grand Theft Auto: Liberty City Stories (2005), the PSP version of the game includes a multiplayer mode through a wireless ad hoc network, which allows up to six players to engage in several different game modes.

cards.heading: A successful return to PSP
cards.text: Vice City Stories received generally positive reviews from critics, and has sold over 7 million copies as of 2026. It is one of the best-selling PlayStation Portable games. The next game in the series was Grand Theft Auto IV, which was released in April 2008.

main.title: Kirby: Squeak Squad
main.summary: Kirby's search for a stolen cake becomes a treasure chase, with copied powers and useful items stored together in a five-slot touch-screen belly.

cards.heading: The game
cards.text: Kirby: Squeak Squad is a 2006 Nintendo DS platform game developed by Flagship with HAL Laboratory, released in Europe as Kirby: Mouse Attack. Kirby's search for a stolen strawberry shortcake draws him into a contest with the treasure-hunting Squeaks, adding pursuits and a touch-screen inventory to the series' familiar movement and Copy Abilities.

cards.heading: A chest turns exploration into a chase
cards.text: Treasure chests are carried through a stage and opened after Kirby reaches its end. The large ones attract the Squeaks, who attack as soon as Kirby picks up a prize they want. A room previously searched at leisure can become a chase through enemies and obstacles, with the chest still needing to reach safety. Finding the treasure is only the first part of the task: the route back out and the ability Kirby is carrying can determine whether he keeps it.

cards.heading: Keep a useful power for later
cards.text: The lower screen shows Kirby's Copy Palette, with space for five bubble items or treasure chests. Touching a stored ability equips it, and touching a food item uses it, so something found earlier can solve a problem encountered much later. Sliding bubbles together mixes them into another item or ability. Keeping a reserve also means managing space: carrying several treasures leaves fewer slots for food and powers, turning the belly into a small inventory that changes throughout the stage.

cards.heading: Change the room with an ability
cards.text: Abilities affect the scenery as well as the enemies. Fire can burn through trees and Ice can freeze water, making a power useful for reaching something that ordinary movement cannot. Bubble turns enemies into items that Kirby can store for later, connecting the action on the upper screen to the inventory below. Looking for hidden treasure encourages a second reading of familiar rooms: a blocked route may be an invitation to return with another power rather than simply the edge of the level.

main.title: Call of Duty 3
main.subtitle: Four Allied armies fight through Normandy
main.summary: Treyarch follows American, British, Canadian and Polish soldiers through the 1944 Normandy campaign, combining infantry combat, vehicles and close encounters.

cards.heading: Four perspectives on the Normandy campaign
cards.text: Call of Duty 3 first appeared in North America on 7 November 2006 for PlayStation 2, Xbox and Xbox 360, with PlayStation 3 and Wii editions following. Developed by Treyarch and published by Activision, it concentrates on Normandy in 1944 rather than moving between distant theatres. Fourteen missions alternate between American, British, Canadian and Polish soldiers, with infantry fighting, tank operations and support for the French Resistance. The main game was made for consoles and did not receive a PC edition.

cards.heading: Grenades can be thrown back
cards.text: The familiar combination of two carried firearms, smoke grenades and recovery behind cover returns, but live enemy grenades can now be picked up and thrown back. Scripted close encounters require the player to struggle with an opponent, while planting explosives involves several actions rather than a single abstract command. Alongside these moments, objectives still include moving through defended positions, operating tanks and marking targets for air strikes.

cards.heading: Larger online battles depend on the console
cards.text: Multiplayer brings Allied and Axis teams together on battlefields with infantry and vehicles, but the editions differ. Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3 support online matches with up to twenty-four players, while Xbox and PlayStation 2 allow sixteen. The Wii edition has no multiplayer. These differences make the platform part of the experience: the same Normandy campaign appeared across two console generations, while their online battles did not share identical limits or features.

main.title: Lumines II
main.subtitle: A puzzle keeps time with another playlist
main.summary: Lumines II is Q Entertainment's PSP puzzle game, first released in North America on 7 November 2006. Falling blocks contain four squares whose colours must be arranged into larger matching groups. A Time Line sweeps across the board, clearing completed groups in time with the music. The sequel expands the original's collection of visual and musical skins, including licensed recordings and videos. A familiar arrangement problem therefore changes its atmosphere as the session continues, with the sound and moving line giving the player another rhythm through which to read the board.

cards.heading: A puzzle keeps time with another playlist
cards.text: Lumines II is Q Entertainment's PSP puzzle game, first released in North America on 7 November 2006. Falling blocks contain four squares whose colours must be arranged into larger matching groups. A Time Line sweeps across the board, clearing completed groups in time with the music. The sequel expands the original's collection of visual and musical skins, including licensed recordings and videos. A familiar arrangement problem therefore changes its atmosphere as the session continues, with the sound and moving line giving the player another rhythm through which to read the board.

cards.heading: The group has to wait for the line
cards.text: A matching square does not disappear as soon as it is formed. It remains until the Time Line reaches it, allowing further blocks to enlarge the cleared area before that moment arrives. This delay creates the game's particular tension: the player is preparing a future result while new pieces continue to demand space. Clearing several groups together raises the reward, but a crowded board leaves fewer safe placements. Music helps make the line's movement predictable, turning timing into part of a puzzle whose individual blocks can be understood at a glance.

cards.heading: More ways to arrange the same central idea
cards.text: Mission mode offers specific challenges, Skin Edit changes the sequence of presentation and the Sequencer provides another musical activity beside the main puzzle. Tetsuya Mizuguchi wanted the sequel to feel like a different party, broadening the soundtrack with artists such as New Order, Missy Elliott and Beck. Reviewers welcomed the added features while differing over the licensed song selection. Katsumi Yokota and Takayuki Nakamura contributed music and design. Lumines II develops a simple relationship rather than replacing it: the blocks supply the problem, and the music helps determine when its solution becomes visible.

main.title: Guitar Hero II
main.subtitle: Two guitars, shared songs and a place to practise the solo
main.summary: Harmonix expanded Guitar Hero with cooperative lead and bass or rhythm parts, and a practice mode for difficult passages.

cards.heading: A second guitar joins the stage
cards.text: Released first for PlayStation 2 on November 7, 2006, Guitar Hero II kept the pleasure of turning a familiar riff into a physical sequence of fretting and strumming. Harmonix added cooperative play: one player takes the lead guitar while another follows the bass or rhythm part. The original PlayStation 2 selection contains 64 songs, combining licensed rock songs, many newly recorded as covers, with bonus tracks. The Xbox 360 edition followed in April 2007 with additional material and an X-Plorer controller.

cards.heading: Learning the difficult passage
cards.text: Practice mode lets players isolate a passage, slow it down and work towards the full tempo. Improved hammer-ons and pull-offs make flowing phrases more comfortable, while three-note chords add another demand. Repeating a difficult section turns listening, coordination and memory into a challenge the player can break down and practise.
